name: TerraPraxis
beneficiaries_note: Our build: from the model's rows at the defaults, about seven tenths of the value is money for power customers where reactors are built (China about 60%, other countries about 33%, India about 7%), the rest the tonnes (heat deaths world-wide, air pollution by coal capacity times smoke per tonne: China and India).
summary: TerraPraxis, a US non-profit with a small UK sister company, designs, convenes and builds software to re-power the world's coal plants with advanced nuclear reactors (its REPOWER consortium), and makes the case for advanced nuclear more broadly (the Ten-Terawatt Initiative). This model counts what its 2022-2024 work ($6.3M) adds to a yardstick, a third of the COP28 pledge to triple nuclear capacity, read at about 2040 (the middle of the years counted), a tenth of it on coal sites, crediting all groups' non-commercial enabling work with 1.5% of that deployment and TerraPraxis with 8% of that work on coal sites and 0.6% elsewhere. Besides the tonnes, the deployment changes what people pay for power: reactors on coal sites are cheaper to build (DOE: 15%-35%), while at the site's discount rate new reactors' power costs about as much as the coal and gas it replaces and, in India, more than the wind and solar it replaces (IEA/NEA projections, with wind and solar's system costs); since most reactors would be built in China and other middle-income countries, where a dollar is worth far more to those paying it, the coal sites' construction savings outweigh the tonnes (in India they are largely offset by nuclear's cost over the wind and solar it replaces). At the defaults a dollar given comes to 0.015 years of healthy life per $1,000, about seven tenths of it from those savings. It is mostly uncertainty: nothing has been built yet, every step from the work to a reactor is a judgment, and the sign turns on what nuclear power will cost against what it replaces; both lines are discounted for missing data.

source.quote: Global coal capacity rose to 2,175 GW, up 259 GW since the Paris Agreement was signed in 2015.

rows.explainer: Coal repowering line. The fleet TerraPraxis's REPOWER work is aimed at: every coal plant in the world, three quarters of them in Asia.

rows.label: Share of coal plant capacity on sites that could host advanced reactors

source.title: US Department of Energy, Office of Nuclear Energy (12 September 2022), Could the nation's coal plant sites help drive a clean energy transition?
source.quote: 80% of the potential sites, with over 250 GW of generating capacity, are suitable for hosting advanced nuclear power plants.

rows.explainer: DOE's national laboratories screened 394 retired and operating US coal sites and found four in five suitable for advanced reactors. No such screening exists for the rest of the world: Asian plants are younger and larger, but many sit in denser or more seismic places. The US share stands in, with the range widened to 50%-90%.

rows.label: Share of the new reactors built by about 2050 that stand on coal sites
rows.explainer: In late 2026 no coal plant has been converted anywhere; the first reactor at a coal site, TerraPower's Natrium plant beside the Naughton coal plant in Wyoming, is under construction for about 2030. Coal sites offer a grid connection, cooling water, land and staff, and four in five US sites could host advanced reactors (DOE 2022), saving 15%-35% of construction cost; but most announced reactors are at existing nuclear sites, data centres and industrial sites. Our judgment, a tenth of the new reactors built (4% to 25%), never more than the suitable coal capacity.

rows.explainer: Tripling 2020's capacity means adding twice that much by 2050 (ignoring reactors retired in between, which the built share below absorbs).

rows.label: Advanced nuclear: share of the tripling pathway that gets built
rows.explainer: The pledge is a target (more than 20 countries signed at launch), not a forecast. Reference class: the 1970s build wave, when most US orders were cancelled, and recent Western projects (Vogtle, Flamanville, Hinkley Point C) years late and far over budget, against China's steady build and the new pull from data centres. The International Energy Agency's own net-zero analysis, quoted in the declaration, has capacity a little more than doubling rather than tripling. Our judgment, 35% (15% to 70%) of the added capacity.

rows.label: New nuclear capacity built on the tripling pathway
Coal repowering: gigawatts of new reactors on coal sites
rows.explainer: A share of the reactors actually built, never more than the suitable coal capacity, so both lines rest on the same build-out.

rows.label: Advanced nuclear: gigawatts built away from coal sites
rows.explainer: The built capacity less the coal-site reactors counted in the repowering line, so no reactor is counted twice; it can't go below zero, since the coal-site share is a share of the same build.

rows.label: Advanced nuclear: tonnes of CO₂e a year those reactors would avert if each replaced coal
rows.explainer: Measured against coal for comparability with the line above, with the supply methane; the counterfactual row below says how much cleaner the grid the reactors join is.

rows.label: Share of the displaced tonnes that are coal's (the rest gas's)
rows.explainer: The power the reactors replace in the 2040s is a mix of coal and gas; coal emits about twice the CO₂ per MWh, so it carries most of the tonnes even where it is under half the energy. Asia's grids, where most of the tonnes fall, still lean on coal. Our judgment, 60% (30% to 90%) of the tonnes.

rows.label: Methane from coal mining, in CO₂e, per tonne of CO₂ from burning coal

source.title: IEA (2025), Global Methane Tracker 2025: understanding methane emissions
source.page: Coal: more than 40 Mt of methane in 2024, including over 4 Mt from abandoned mines

rows.explainer: About 40 million tonnes of methane a year from coal (IEA) × 29.8 (methane's 100-year warming potential, IPCC AR6) = 1.2 billion tonnes of CO₂e, against roughly 15 billion tonnes of CO₂ from burning coal (about two fifths of the world's 37 billion tonnes of energy CO₂): 7.7%. Abandoned mines (4 Mt) keep leaking, so not all of it stops with the coal; range 5% to 10%.

rows.label: Methane from gas supply, in CO₂e, per tonne of CO₂ from burning gas

source.title: IEA (2025), Global Methane Tracker 2025: understanding methane emissions
source.page: Natural gas operations: nearly 35 Mt of methane in 2024

rows.explainer: About 35 million tonnes of methane a year from gas operations (IEA) × 29.8 = 1.0 billion tonnes of CO₂e, against roughly 7.4 billion tonnes of CO₂ from burning gas (about a fifth of the world's energy CO₂): 14%. Leaks scale only partly with the gas burned; range 8% to 20%.

rows.label: CO₂e of the displaced power's supply methane, per tonne of its CO₂
rows.explainer: Mine methane on the coal tonnes and supply-chain methane on the gas tonnes, weighted by their shares of the displaced tonnes.

rows.label: Share of the deployment due to the period's enabling work (all non-commercial groups together)
rows.explainer: TerraPraxis wins no laws: it designs, convenes and builds tools (standard designs for re-powering a coal plant with Bryden Wood, software with Microsoft, AI licensing tools, the REPOWER consortium of utilities, vendors, financiers and governments, the Ten-Terawatt Initiative). Whether reactors are built turns mostly on cost, finance, demand and policy. Reference class: our model of Clean Air Task Force credits all advocates' nuclear policy wins of 2022-2025 (the ADVANCE Act, the tripling pledges, state laws) with 5% × 30% = 1.5% of the deployment. Enabling work of the same years (designs, studies, tools, convening by national laboratories, the IAEA, EPRI, think tanks and NGOs) is a channel of about the same weight: less proven than a law, but aimed at the cost and siting barriers that decide deployment. Our judgment, 1.5% (0.5% to 5%) over the three years, for both lines. A share of a broad trend, not one bet, so no single-event tag.

rows.label: Years the result counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The site's one answer (docs/normalization.md 2.9): speeding a technology brings its tonnes forward by the shared number of years.

rows.label: Coal repowering: expected tonnes before adjustments
Advanced nuclear: expected tonnes before adjustments
Expected tonnes a year of the period, before adjustments
rows.explainer: The two lines' expected tonnes, summed and spread over the period's three years.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment: how far the pathway tonnes and the enabling share should be trusted
rows.explainer: The tonnes come from yardsticks (a pledge, a site screening) and judgments, not from a regulator's assessment of a won rule; nuclear projections have run ahead of what was built for fifty years, and that a design or convening programme moves deployment at all is untested. Anchor: our model of Clean Air Task Force takes 0.8 for regulators' estimates of won rules; this is lower because nothing here has been won or measured. Our judgment, 0.7 (0.4 to 1.0), for both lines.

rows.label: Coal repowering: share of coal-site reactors that are extra nuclear, not reactors that would have been built elsewhere
rows.explainer: Much of repowering's value is siting: a reactor at a coal site is cheaper (15%-35% less to build, DOE 2022) and faster to connect, so some reactors move there from other sites rather than being added. The cost saving also makes some reactors happen that otherwise wouldn't, and repowering lets a utility keep its site, staff and grid rights. Our judgment, 40% (15% to 70%) extra.

rows.label: Coal repowering: CO₂ per MWh of the power the extra reactors replace, relative to coal
rows.explainer: Where repowering retires a coal unit early it saves the full coal tonne; where the coal would have closed anyway it saves only what would have replaced it (in the US, about a quarter of coal's CO₂ per MWh: facts: climate.us_coal_replacement_tco2_per_mwh). Repowering is aimed at Asia's young coal fleets, where the alternative to repowering is often more years of coal. Our judgment, 50% (25% to 80%) of a coal MWh's CO₂ in the 2040s.

rows.label: Coal repowering: share of the coal tonnes that are a real cut
rows.explainer: Extra reactors only, each replacing power that emits the share of a coal MWh above.

rows.label: Advanced nuclear: CO₂ per MWh of the power new reactors replace, relative to coal
rows.explainer: New reactors join grids in the late 2030s and 2040s that are cleaner than today's: the world average today is a little under half of a coal MWh's CO₂ and falling as wind and solar grow, faster in Europe and the US than in Asia. Our judgment, 35% (15% to 60%) of coal's tonnes.

rows.label: Coal repowering: TerraPraxis's share of the non-commercial resources behind the enabling work
rows.explainer: TerraPraxis has led coal repowering as an organised idea since 2020 (the REPOWER consortium, standard designs, site-assessment software), on about $2 million a year. Others doing the same kind of work: DOE and its national laboratories (the 2022 coal-to-nuclear study and later site work), the IAEA, EPRI, the Nuclear Innovation Alliance, Clean Air Task Force, the World Nuclear Association, and utilities' own studies; reactor vendors' business development is commercial and sits outside this share. No source sizes the field's budgets, so the range is wide: our judgment, 8% (2% to 25%) of the resources.

rows.label: Advanced nuclear: TerraPraxis's share of the non-commercial resources behind the enabling work
rows.explainer: Its broader advanced nuclear work (the Ten-Terawatt Initiative, launched in 2024 and its white paper presented at Davos in January 2025, AI licensing tools with Microsoft, papers on industrial heat and shipping) is a small part of a large field: the Nuclear Energy Institute, Clean Air Task Force's $5 million a year on advanced nuclear, ClearPath, the Breakthrough Institute, Third Way, the World Nuclear Association, the IAEA and the OECD Nuclear Energy Agency, and governments' own deployment programmes. No source sizes the field's budgets, so the range is wide: our judgment, 0.6% (0.1% to 3%).

rows.label: Other work not in the two lines (geothermal, energy modelling), as a share of the modelled value
rows.explainer: Synthetic fuels, industrial heat and shipping are uses of the reactors in the advanced nuclear line. What remains is small: advanced geothermal and energy-system modelling, each a page of the website and a few reports. Their spending is in the cost, so leaving them out would count them as worth nothing. Our judgment, 5% of the modelled net value (0 to 15%), the same kind of work as the rest.

rows.label: Side effect: accident, waste and proliferation risk from more reactors, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Nuclear power's deaths per unit of electricity, accidents and waste included, are about as low as wind's and solar's and far below fossil fuels' (Markandya & Wilkinson 2007). TerraPraxis's tonnes come largely from reactors in Asia and in countries new to nuclear power, where regulators are younger and proliferation worries larger than in the US. Our judgment, −0.5% of the modelled value (−2% to 0).

rows.label: Side effect: jobs and tax revenue kept in coal towns, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: A re-powered plant keeps a coal town's jobs and tax base: DOE's case study counts more than 650 permanent jobs at one converted site. Most of these jobs would exist somewhere else (a reactor built elsewhere, other work), so only the gain from keeping them in place counts, a small amount of income beside the tonnes. Our judgment, +0.3% of the modelled value (0 to 1%).

rows.label: Share of the new reactors built in China

source.title: IEA (2026), Global Energy Review 2026: nuclear
source.quote: Half of capacity under construction globally is in China.

rows.explainer: Where the reactors are built decides who pays for them. Half of the 78 GW under construction worldwide is in China (IEA); China's build is steady and state-planned, while the pledge's growth elsewhere is less certain. Our judgment, 45% (30% to 60%) of the reactors built to 2050, for both lines.

rows.label: Share of the new reactors built in India

source.title: IEA (2026), Global Energy Review 2026: nuclear
source.quote: Egypt, India and Türkiye each have around 5 GW under construction.

rows.explainer: India has about 5 of the 78 GW under construction (6%) and plans a large expansion; it also has the world's second-largest coal fleet, so coal repowering matters there. Our judgment, 10% (4% to 20%).

rows.label: Share of the new reactors built in the United States
rows.explainer: Almost nothing is under construction in the US today, but DOE's pathway (200 GW by 2050) and data-centre demand point to a large share later if costs fall. Our judgment, 15% (5% to 30%).

rows.label: Share of the new reactors built in other middle-income countries (Türkiye, Egypt, newcomers)

source.title: IEA (2026), Global Energy Review 2026: nuclear
source.quote: Egypt, India and Türkiye each have around 5 GW under construction.

rows.explainer: Egypt and Türkiye each have about 5 GW under construction, about 10 of the 34 GW outside China and India (IEA), and several middle-income newcomers plan reactors. Our judgment, 10% (5% to 20%) of the build, valued at China's survey-scale consumption and costs as an upper-middle-income stand-in (cheap sun and wind, reactors built by Russian, Chinese and Korean vendors at near-Chinese costs).

rows.label: Share of a reactor's construction cost saved by reusing a coal site

source.title: US Department of Energy, Office of Nuclear Energy (12 September 2022), Could the nation's coal plant sites help drive a clean energy transition?
source.quote: reusing coal infrastructure for new, advanced nuclear reactors can save around 15-35% in construction costs.

rows.explainer: DOE's national laboratories' estimate for reusing a coal plant's grid connection, cooling, buildings and land; the middle of their range.

rows.label: Coal repowering: construction cost saved on reactors moved to coal sites, units of value
rows.formula: rep_gw_repowered * pathway_counted_share * p_success * (1 - rep_additional_share) * rep_attribution_share * 1e6 * rep_site_cost_saving * w_overnight * @cpi.usa_2024 / @cpi.usa_2018 * (1 - (1 + $discount_rate) ^ -years_of_impact) * wait_discount * evidence_adj * missing_data_adj * $uov_per_ln_consumption / @public_funds.compliance_cost_payer_multiple
rows.explainer: The reactors the counterfactual treats as moved from other sites still save their builders and customers the coal site's construction saving. Credited gigawatts moved (the line's chance, share not extra, TerraPraxis's share) × the saving × each region's overnight cost over its payers' consumption (row above), in 2024 dollars; the saving would have come anyway once the shared years counted are over, so only bringing it forward counts (1 − (1 + rate)^−years), after the shared wait, with the evidence and missing-data steps. Valued as money gained by those who pay for power, at the shared payer multiple (docs/normalization.md 2.21).

rows.label: Extra reactors: cost of their power over what it replaces, units of value
rows.formula: -pathway_counted_share * p_success * twh_per_gw_year * 1e6 * @cpi.usa_2024 / @cpi.usa_2018 * discounted_years * evidence_adj * missing_data_adj * $uov_per_ln_consumption / @public_funds.compliance_cost_payer_multiple * (rep_gw_repowered * rep_additional_share * rep_attribution_share * (w_gap_rep - rep_site_cost_saving * w_investment) + nuc_gw_not_coal * nuc_attribution_share * w_gap_nuc)
rows.explainer: The credited extra reactors' output (MWh a year) × their cost over what they replace: the fossil and clean parts at each region's gaps (rows above), and the coal-site reactors less the site's construction saving per MWh; each region over its payers' consumption, in 2024 dollars, over the same discounted years as the tonnes, with the evidence and missing-data steps; valued as money lost (or gained, if negative) by those who pay for power (docs/normalization.md 2.21).

rows.label: Money effects of the deployment, units of value per year of the period
rows.explainer: The siting savings and the extra power cost, per year of the period, in the main chain through the bridge below (docs/normalization.md 2.21).

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths per tonne of coal power displaced in the 2040s, relative to the fossil-fuel average

source.title: Markandya & Wilkinson (2007), Electricity generation and health, The Lancet 370(9591), 979-990
source.page: Table 2: deaths per TWh from air pollution and accidents, Europe (lignite 32.6, coal 24.6, oil 18.4, gas 2.8)

rows.explainer: The shared rate is 146 air-pollution deaths per million tonnes of fossil CO₂ (climate.deaths_per_tco2e_air_pollution), about 146 per TWh of coal power at a tonne per MWh. Anchors: European coal 24.6 deaths per TWh in Markandya & Wilkinson (0.17 of the average); US coal plants today about 10 per million tonnes (climate.us_coal_power_smoke_factor, 0.067, the low end); burden studies of China's and India's coal power (GBD MAPS) put Chinese coal near 0.15 and Indian near 0.55 (the high end). The tonnes come in the late 2030s and 2040s, mostly in Asia, with more pollution controls than today. Our judgment, 0.22 (0.07 to 0.55).

rows.label: The deployment's money effects, in tonnes of CO₂e
rows.formula: money_uov_per_year / (($deaths_per_tco2e * $climate_heat_share * ((1 - methane_share) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ -$climate_heat_death_delay + methane_share * @climate.methane_heat_deaths_vs_co2 * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ -@climate.methane_heat_death_delay) * (1 + $side_effect_weight * @climate.nondeath_damages_vs_deaths) * (@death_ages.heat_share_under5 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_under5 + @death_ages.heat_share_5_14 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_5_14 + @death_ages.heat_share_15_49 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_15_49 + @death_ages.heat_share_50plus * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_50_74) + ($deaths_per_tco2e * (1 - $climate_heat_share) * air_pollution_weight + extra_deaths_per_tco2e + methane_share * @climate.ozone_deaths_per_tco2e_methane / (1 + ln(1 + $discount_rate) * @climate.methane_lifetime_years)) * (@death_ages.air_pollution_share_under5 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_under5 + @death_ages.air_pollution_share_5_14 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_5_14 + @death_ages.air_pollution_share_15_49 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_15_49 + @death_ages.air_pollution_share_50plus * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_50_74)) * $life_value_multiplier)
rows.explainer: Units of value into tonnes at what a tonne of these is worth on the site's scale (its heat and air-pollution deaths by age, as the conversion counts them), the bridge the other climate models use (docs/normalization.md 2.6).

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂e averted per year of the period
rows.formula: ((rep_downstream * rep_total_adj + nuc_downstream * nuc_total_adj) / period_years * (1 + nuclear_harm_share + community_continuity_share) + tco2e_from_uov) * (1 + unmodelled_benefits_adj)
rows.explainer: Each line's expected tonnes × its own adjustments, summed and spread over the period's three years, with the side effects added as shares and the money effects through the bridge; the other work's share applies to the net.
